analysis.one_liner: Repeals the Americans with Disabilities Act, removing civil rights protections for disabled people.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one representative with no cosponsors, sat in four House committees and its subcommittees until the Congress ended without ever getting a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: A single House member proposed erasing the Americans with Disabilities Act of 1990, the federal law that bans discrimination against people with disabilities in jobs, public services, and public accommodations, and requires reasonable accommodations like ramps and accessible workplaces. Repealing it would have stripped millions of disabled Americans of those legal protections. The bill had no cosponsors and was referred to four committees; none ever acted on it, and it died when the 102nd Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, employers and businesses that provide public accommodations would have been freed from the ADA's requirements: no obligation to provide reasonable accommodations to disabled workers, no accessible-entry and service requirements, and no federal ban on disability discrimination in hiring and firing. Businesses facing accommodation or accessibility costs would have gained the most.

how_it_helps.text: The bill repeals the ADA in its entirety, a one-sentence bill eliminating the federal prohibition on disability discrimination in employment, government services, and places of public accommodation [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, people with disabilities would have borne the cost: losing legal recourse against workplace discrimination, losing the right to reasonable accommodations on the job, and losing accessibility requirements in stores, transportation, and public services. Family members and taxpayers could also have faced higher costs as disabled people lost employment and independence.

drawbacks.text: Repealing the ADA would have removed legal recourse for disabled workers facing hiring and firing discrimination, with no replacement protections [S3].

Supporters of the bill's underlying aim argued the ADA imposes compliance costs on businesses, particularly smaller firms, for ramps, equipment, and accommodations; full repeal would have eliminated those obligations but also the protections those costs buy.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: Any benefit to businesses avoiding accommodation and accessibility costs would have come directly at the expense of disabled Americans' civil rights, employment access, and physical access to public life. There was no offsetting benefit to the public in the bill; it was a clean repeal with no replacement.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to four House committees and then to five subcommittees, none of which took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Representative Mickey Edwards of Oklahoma introduced the bill alone on June 22, 1992, with no cosponsors [S1][S3][S4].
It was referred the same day to four committees: Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, Public Works and Transportation, and Judiciary [S1][S5].

Over the following two months it was parceled out to five subcommittees, including Civil and Constitutional Rights, Surface Transportation, and Employment Opportunities, but no committee or subcommittee ever held a markup or vote [S5].
The bill died with the 102nd Congress on January 3, 1993, and the Americans with Disabilities Act remains law [S1][S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained; people with disabilities kept their federal civil rights protections, and the bill's lone sponsor failed to attract any support.

for.name: Rep. Mickey Edwards
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to repeal the ADA alone, with no cosponsors.

against.name: House committees of referral (Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, Public Works and Transportation, Judiciary)
against.role: Committees the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled the bill for consideration; it sat in committee and subcommittee referral until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: There was no recorded vote and no cosponsors from either party; the bill never advanced far enough to reveal a partisan split, though its sole sponsor was a Republican [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Employers and public accommodations (retail, restaurants, transit providers)
industries.note: Repeal would have freed businesses from ADA accommodation and accessibility requirements, lowering their compliance costs by shifting those costs onto disabled people through lost jobs and access. The bill died, so businesses remain subject to the law.

industries.industry: Accessibility and construction trades (ramps, lifts, accessible equipment)
industries.note: Repeal would have eliminated demand for accessibility modifications required by the ADA. The bill's death preserved that market.
